1.overview: A functional dependency α → β on schema R means: whenever two tuples agree on α, they must agree on β in every legal instance. This is Armstrong's definition used for normalization theory and inference axioms. Normalization and decomposition are processes that use FDs; set theory is too broad. The named concept is functional dependency (D).

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Normalization". Normalization reorganizes relations to reduce redundancy using FDs and keys, but it is not the definition of an FD itself. Students confuse the tool (normalization) with the rule (dependency).
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Decomposition". Decomposition splits schemas to eliminate anomalies; again it applies FDs rather than naming them.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Set Theory". Set theory underlies relations mathematically, yet exams ask for the specific database dependency term.
options.D: Option D (CORRECT): "Functional Dependency". This is the standard answer: FDs capture constraints like {StudentID} → {StudentName} in university schemas.

1.studyTip: Remember: FD = same α values force same β values in all legal relations.

2.overview: Saltzer and Schroeder's design principles guide secure systems. Economy of mechanism demands simple, small implementations to reduce bugs and audit surface. Least privilege limits rights; fail-safe defaults set safe states; open design assumes algorithms are public while keys stay secret. Small-and-simple maps to economy of mechanism (C).

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Fail-safe Defaults". Fail-safe defaults require that access defaults to denial unless explicitly granted—different principle.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Least privilege". Least privilege says each subject gets minimum rights needed—orthogonal to simplicity of mechanism.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "Economy of Mechanism". Economy of mechanism literally means keep security code tiny and reviewable—matches the stem.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Open Design". Open design (Kerckhoffs) is about public algorithms, not minimal code size.

2.studyTip: Map 'small and simple security code' → Economy of Mechanism on Ethiopian exams.

3.overview: Qualitative architecture analysis (ATAM, SAAM) evaluates tradeoffs among quality attributes using scenarios: stimulus, environment, response, and measures. Team size and org charts are managerial, not architectural drivers. Log files help operations post-deployment but do not structure design tradeoffs. Quality scenarios (C) are standard.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Team size". Team size affects delivery velocity, not a formal architecture evaluation artifact.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Organizational structures". Org structure influences communication paths but not scenario-based quality reasoning.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "Quality scenarios". Quality scenarios document concrete stimuli (e.g., 1000 users) and expected responses—core ATAM input.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Log files". Logs are runtime artifacts; qualitative analysis happens before or during design reviews.

3.studyTip: ATAM keyword: quality scenarios drive qualitative architecture evaluation.

4.overview: Selection sort performs at most one swap per outer pass to place the minimum element, giving n−1 swaps for n>1. Unlike bubble sort, swaps are bounded by passes, not comparisons. Answer B (n−1).

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "n - 2". n−2 swaps might occur in edge cases but is not the tight maximum taught in curricula.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "n - 1". Classic result: each of n−1 passes may swap once → at most n−1 swaps.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "n". n swaps over-count; selection sort does not swap every comparison.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "n / 2". n/2 is not the established upper bound for selection sort swaps.

4.studyTip: Selection sort max swaps = n − 1 (one per pass except the last).

5.overview: OOP separates behavior (methods) from state (fields) inside objects. C++ and Java are OO languages; Java is not the only OO language. Statement C falsely claims OOP does not separate behavior from data—that is the NOT-correct statement.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "C++ is an object-oriented programming language". True: C++ supports classes, inheritance, and polymorphism.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Java is an object-oriented programming language". True: Java is object-oriented with classes and interfaces.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "The object-oriented approach does not separate the behavior of a system from the data". False claim: encapsulation explicitly separates interface (behavior) from representation (data).
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Java is the only object-oriented programming language". Also false in practice (C++, Python, C# exist), but C is the classic textbook wrong statement about OOP definition.

5.studyTip: NOT-correct OOP question: denying behavior/data separation is the usual trap answer (C).

6.overview: Testers and developers share quality goals but different tactics. Collaboration reduces defect cost, improves reproducibility, and avoids adversarial blame. On-time delivery or zero defects alone are unrealistic single-team promises.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "To ensure that the project is completed on time". Schedule pressure is project-management scope; good relations help but are not primarily for deadlines.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "To foster collaboration and communication between the two teams". Communication and collaboration align expectations on reproducible bugs and fixes—best answer.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "To make sure that the software is defect-free". Defect-free software is impossible; testing reduces risk, not eliminates it.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "To reduce the cost of the project". Cost reduction may follow quality, but it is not the primary reason for healthy tester–developer relations.

7.overview: Wireless encoding, modulation, and frequency bands belong to the Physical layer (Layer 1) in OSI. MAC/Medium access is layer 2; application and LLC are higher. Exam lists Physical as D.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Application Layer". Application layer handles HTTP/DNS semantics, not radio frequencies.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Logical Link Control Layer". LLC is part of data link—framing and flow on LANs, not RF modulation.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Medium Access Layer". Medium access resembles MAC sublayer, still not primary for frequency band definition.
options.D: Option D (CORRECT): "Physical Layer". Physical layer defines bit transmission over the medium—including wireless radio parameters.

7.studyTip: Wireless signal encoding → OSI Physical layer.

8.overview: Layered architectures separate concerns (presentation, business, persistence), improving maintainability and change isolation. They may add indirection that hurts raw performance or runtime plug-in flexibility. Modifiability during development is the usual win (A).

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "Flexibility in modifying or changing the system". Changing one layer with stable interfaces reduces ripple effects—primary benefit in textbooks.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Runtime efficiency (performance)". Extra layers can add latency; performance often degrades unless carefully optimized.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Flexibility at runtime (configurability)". Runtime configurability is a deployment concern, not the classic layered benefit.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Non-repudiability". Non-repudiation is a security service, unrelated to layering structure.

8.studyTip: Layered architecture improves changeability/modifiability of the system (A).

9.overview: SRS quality attributes include consistency (no contradictions), completeness, verifiability, and unambiguity. The stem defines consistency: no conflicting requirements subsets. Label: Consistent (A).

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "Consistent". Matches the definition given—requirements do not conflict.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Verifiable". Verifiable means each requirement can be tested—different property.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Unambiguous". Unambiguous means one interpretation—related but not identical to consistency.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Correct". Correctness is not the standard name for non-conflict in IEEE SRS checklists.

9.studyTip: No conflicting requirements in SRS → consistency.

10.overview: Software architecture documents early decisions, enables stakeholder communication, and provides transferable abstractions for reuse across products. All listed benefits are textbook motivations—answer D (All of the above).

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Communication among stakeholders". Stakeholder communication via views and diagrams is a core architecture benefit.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Early design decisions". Early design decisions are costly to change later—architecture captures them explicitly.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Transferable abstraction of a system". Transferable abstractions (patterns, styles) speed new product development.
options.D: Option D (CORRECT): "All of the above". Combines A–C; architecture serves all these roles simultaneously.

10.studyTip: Why architecture matters: communication, early decisions, abstraction → All of the above.

11.overview: Android Services run in the background. stopSelf() lets a service stop itself; Context.stopService() stops from outside. finish() ends Activities; System.exit() is inappropriate on Android.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "By using the stopSelt() and stopService() method". Correct pair for terminating started services.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "By using the finish() method". finish() closes an Activity UI, not a Service lifecycle.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "By using system.exit() method". System.exit() kills the VM—avoid on Android; use proper component APIs.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "None of the above". There is a valid API—A is correct, so not 'none'.

11.studyTip: Stop Android services: stopSelf() and stopService() (A).

12.overview: Quantitative architecture analysis uses structural metrics: coupling, cohesion, cyclomatic complexity, and dependency cycles. High coupling between modules predicts change amplification and defect clusters. Comment quality is subjective.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Missing comments". Missing comments may indicate poor documentation but are weak quantitative architecture metrics.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Names of public methods do not reflect their purpose". Method naming helps readability, not a standard architecture metric like coupling.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Number of test cases per component". Test count per component varies by strategy; not the primary architecture smell indicator.
options.D: Option D (CORRECT): "High coupling of components". High coupling is a classic architecture problem metric measurable from dependency graphs.

12.studyTip: Architecture smell metric: high coupling between components (D).

13.overview: Polymorphism allows one interface, many implementations: same method name, different behavior (overriding/overloading). Public methods or hiding alone describe encapsulation, not polymorphism.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Declaring all the methods of a class as public". Making all methods public breaks encapsulation; not polymorphism.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Declaring all the attributes of a class as private". Private attributes are encapsulation, not polymorphism.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Hiding information so it is not accessible to other classes". Information hiding is encapsulation/abstraction.
options.D: Option D (CORRECT): "Having methods or operators with the same name performing different functions". Same name, different behavior across types/operators defines polymorphism.

14.overview: ContentProvider exposes structured data with URIs for cross-app sharing (contacts, media). Intents pass messages between components; databases are storage behind providers.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "For entering data in the database". Entering DB data is done via SQLite/Room APIs, not the provider's main purpose.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "For sharing data between applications". Sharing between applications via URIs and permissions is the canonical use.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "For passing data from one Activity to another". Activity-to-Activity data typically uses Intent extras, not providers.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "None of the above". B is correct, so 'none' is wrong.

14.studyTip: Android ContentProvider → share data between apps (B).

15.overview: In ER modeling, cardinality ratio (1:1, 1:N, M:N) states how many entities on one side relate to the other. Participation constraints are optional/mandatory membership; degree counts relationship arity.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "Cardinality ratio". Cardinality ratio directly answers 'how many associated entities'.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Limited ratio". Not standard terminology.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Degree ratio". Degree of relationship is number of participating entity sets (binary vs ternary).
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Participation constraints". Participation (total/partial) differs from numeric cardinality.

16.overview: With unit step cost, UCS expands by increasing path cost like BFS expands by depth—both explore in non-decreasing cost order and share similar complexity characteristics when costs are uniform. UCS and BFS (C) are the paired answer here.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "BFS and DFS". BFS and DFS differ in completeness on infinite trees and ordering.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "DFS and UCS". DFS and UCS differ dramatically in optimality and fringe management.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "UCS and BFS". Uniform step costs align UCS frontier with BFS layering behavior—exam pairing.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "DFS and BFS". DFS is depth-first; BFS is breadth-first—different fringe policies.

16.studyTip: Equal step cost: UCS behaves like BFS → pair UCS & BFS (C).

17.overview: Boehm's spiral model emphasizes risk-driven iterations: prototypes, simulations, and risk resolution before committing resources. Risk management (C) is the hallmark feature.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "performance management o". Performance management is ongoing ops, not spiral's defining loop.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "efficiency management". Efficiency management is vague and not spiral-specific.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "risk management". Each loop explicitly addresses highest risks first—core spiral idea.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Quality management". Quality management appears in all models; risk drives spiral uniquely.

18.overview: Software testing within QA verifies that the product meets specified requirements and reveals gaps before release. Monitoring lifecycle or controlling cost are management functions, not testing's primary goal.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "To monitor the software development lifecycle". Lifecycle monitoring is PM/CMMI activity, not the test mission.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "To control the cost of software development". Cost control is business management; tests may inform it indirectly.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "To ensure that the software meets the specified requirements". Conformance to requirements is the central testing objective in IEEE/ISTQB views.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "To manage project timelines and deadlines". Schedule management belongs to project managers.

18.studyTip: Main testing goal: verify software meets requirements (C).

19.overview: Recursion occurs when a function calls itself (directly or indirectly via helpers). Base cases prevent infinite regress. Traversal and Polish notation are unrelated algorithmic styles.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "Recursion". Recursive definition matches the stem exactly.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Sub algorithm". Sub-algorithm is generic decomposition, not necessarily self-calls.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Traversal algorithm". Traversal walks structures; Polish notation is expression form.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Polish notation". Polish notation orders operators; not self-calling algorithms.

20.overview: Supervised learning trains on labeled examples (input, correct output). The model learns a mapping to predict labels on new data. Unlabeled training defines unsupervised learning; reinforcement uses rewards.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Reinforcement learning with a reward-based system". Reinforcement learning is a separate paradigm with agents and rewards.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Learning by observing human behavior". Learning by imitation/observation is not the standard supervised definition.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "Training a machine learning model with labeled data". Labeled training data is the defining property of supervised learning.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Training a machine learning model with unlabeled data". Unlabeled data characterizes unsupervised clustering and association.

21.overview: Operating systems schedule processes, manage memory and I/O, and provide system calls. Compilers translate HLL to machine code—that is a language tool chain function, not a core OS duty. Answer B.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Runs software utilities and programs". Running utilities is part of providing execution environment.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Translates high-level programming language into machine code". Compilation is typically done by gcc/javac, not the kernel itself.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Manages computer system resources". Resource management (CPU, memory, devices) is central OS role.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Makes the computer system convenient to use". Convenience for users (shell, filesystem) is an OS goal.

21.studyTip: NOT an OS function: compiling high-level languages (B).

22.overview: Transport demultiplexing uses port numbers with IP addresses to deliver segments to the correct socket/application. CRC/MAC relate to error detection and link addressing, not application binding on a host.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "Port number". Port number plus IP identifies an endpoint for TCP/UDP delivery.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "CRC". CRC detects bit errors; does not select applications.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "MAC address". MAC addresses operate at layer 2 between hops, not end-to-end apps.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "IP address only". IP alone identifies host; port selects application on that host.

22.studyTip: Deliver to correct application → port number lookup (A).

23.overview: IPC mechanisms (pipes, message queues, shared memory with sync) let processes coordinate across protection boundaries. Modern IPC often uses separate address spaces with kernel-mediated copying or mapped pages.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Allows processes to communicate when using the same address space only". Same address space communication is threads/shared memory within a process, not classic IPC across processes.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Allows processes to communicate and synchronize without sharing the same address space". IPC allows communication/synchronization without sharing an address space—canonical definition.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Allows processes to synchronize without communication". Synchronization without communication is incomplete IPC description.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "None of the above". B captures standard IPC; 'none' is incorrect.

23.studyTip: IPC → processes communicate without shared address space (B).

24.overview: The reconstructed snippet reverses via unshift in a loop, rebuilding [22,111,44] from the original order. Trace index-by-index: each unshift prepends, restoring original forward order after reverse iteration.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "[1122, 111, 44]". Garbled OCR numbers; not the logical output of the described loop.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "[44, 111, 22]". Fully reversed array would be [44,111,22] if using push instead of unshift pattern shown.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "[22, 111, 44]". Matches forward original array after reverse-index unshift construction.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "[111]". Single element output ignores full iteration.

24.studyTip: Trace unshift-from-end loops carefully on JS output questions.

25.overview: Verifiability means each requirement can be checked objectively (test, inspection, analysis) within acceptable cost. Complete/traceable/modifiable are separate IEEE SRS qualities.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "complete". Completeness: all needed requirements present.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "traceable". Traceability: links to sources and tests.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "verifiable". Cost-effective checking is verifiability—matches stem.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "modifiable". Modifiable: requirements can be changed cleanly in the document.

25.studyTip: Cost-effective check of each requirement → verifiable SRS (C).

26.overview: A foreign key in a child table references a primary key in a parent (referenced) table, identifying which parent row the child row relates to. The FK value points into the referenced relation.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Parent and child tables simultaneously". FK is not simultaneously identifying rows in both tables with one column.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Referenced (parent) table". Referenced (parent) table row is what the FK value must match.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Child table only". Child holds the FK column, but the semantic target is the referenced row in parent.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "All of the above". Not 'all of the above'—specific direction matters in relational design.

26.studyTip: Foreign key identifies a row in the referenced parent table (B).

27.overview: Running thread yields CPU voluntarily via Thread.yield() (or sleep), entering READY without blocking on I/O. Blocking waits move to BLOCKED/WAITING, not directly READY in all APIs.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "Encountering a yield() call". yield() keeps runnable state READY when scheduled again—matches 'return to READY'.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Encountering a sleep() call". sleep() timed waiting may map to different states depending on OS/API.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Encountering a wait() on a lock". wait() on monitors typically blocks, not a simple READY transition.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Becoming blocked waiting for I/O". I/O block is not voluntary yield to READY from running in the same sense.

27.studyTip: Running → READY via yield (A) on standard thread state charts.

28.overview: View-based architecture documentation (4+1, Rozanski & Woods) commonly includes context, logical/component, process, development, and physical views. Context view shows system boundary and external actors—most frequently cited with component view.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "Context view". Context view is essential in nearly every architecture method.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Configuration view". Configuration view is deployment detail, less universal than context.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Building Block/Component view". Building block/component view is also core; exams often pair with context—A listed first as most common entry.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Physical database view". Physical database view is too narrow for general architecture documentation.

28.studyTip: Frequent architecture views: Context (and Component) — answer Context (A).

29.overview: Risk retention (acceptance) means the organization accepts the risk and does not mitigate it further—budget for losses. Avoidance eliminates exposure; reduction mitigates; transfer uses insurance/contracts.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Risk avoidance". Avoidance stops the risky activity entirely.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Risk retention". Retention = accept occurrence, no further action—matches stem.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Risk reduction". Reduction implements controls to lower probability/impact.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Risk transfer". Transfer shifts financial consequence (insurance).

29.studyTip: Accept risk, do nothing → risk retention (B).

30.overview: ICMP carries error reports (unreachable, time exceeded) and diagnostic messages (echo/ping) at the network layer. It does not perform routing tables or bulk data forwarding—that is IP and transport layers.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "IP addressing". IP addressing is configuration, not ICMP's primary role.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "error and diagnostic functions". Error and diagnostic functions are textbook ICMP purpose.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Data forwarding". Data forwarding is done by IP routers forwarding packets, not ICMP payloads as data plane.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Network routing". Routing protocols (OSPF, BGP) build tables; ICMP assists errors, not primary routing.

31.overview: The 'data explosion' dilemma: organizations collect vast data but struggle to extract actionable knowledge—'too much data, too little knowledge' (D) captures the insight vs. noise problem in KDD.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Too much knowledge and too much data". Too much knowledge is the opposite problem statement.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Too much data and too much opponunlty". Opportunity is vague marketing wording, not the classic DIKW gap phrase.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Distributed knowledge and distributed data". Distributed knowledge describes federated orgs, not the explosion paradox.
options.D: Option D (CORRECT): "too much data too little knowledge". Standard phrase taught in data mining/BI courses for the modern data flood.

31.studyTip: Data explosion sentence → too much data, too little knowledge (D).

32.overview: Android service lifecycle states include created, started, bound; running is operational. 'Destroyed' is not a named lifecycle state—services are destroyed after stop/unbind, but Destroyed is not listed like Activity's destroyed callback state in the same way.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "Destroyed". Destroyed is not a standard enumerated service lifecycle state in early Android curricula.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Running". Running is a valid operational phase.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Start". Start/onStart is part of lifecycle.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Paused". Paused applies more to activities than classic service states.

32.studyTip: NOT a service lifecycle state: Destroyed (A) in many AAU keys.

33.overview: SQL NULL represents missing or unknown value, distinct from zero or empty string. Entity attributes use NULL when unknown.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Not Applicable". N/A is informal; SQL standard uses NULL.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Null". NULL is the relational model answer for missing attribute value.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Default". Default is a chosen value when defined, not absence of value.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Zero". Zero is a concrete value, not unknown.

33.studyTip: Missing attribute value in databases → NULL (B).

34.overview: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time. Quick sort can degrade to O(n²); bubble and selection are O(n²).

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "Merge sort". Merge sort worst-case O(n log n) is optimal among comparison sorts listed.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Selection sort". Selection sort is O(n²) always.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Quick sort". Quick sort worst case O(n²) on bad pivots.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Bubble sort". Bubble sort O(n²) worst case.

34.studyTip: Best worst-case time among choices → merge sort (A).

35.overview: Adaptive maintenance adjusts software to environmental changes (OS, regulations, hardware). Corrective fixes defects; preventive improves future maintainability; perfective adds features.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Perfective maintenance". Perfective adds user-visible features, not environment tracking.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Adaptive maintenance". Adaptive matches evolving external environment—answer.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Preventive maintenance". Preventive reduces future failures (refactoring, docs).
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Corrective maintenance". Corrective repairs discovered bugs.

36.overview: TCP reliability uses acknowledgments and retransmission timers so the sender knows data arrived. Bits/buffers/frames are mechanisms but ACKs are the verification signal named in the stem.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "Acknowledgment". ACK numbers confirm cumulative receipt—core reliability.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Bits". Bits are physical representation, not the verification protocol element asked.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Buffer". Buffers store data; do not by themselves verify arrival to peer.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Frame". Frames are link-layer packaging; TCP ACK is transport-layer confirmation.

37.overview: ISTQB fundamental test process: planning, analysis/design, implementation/execution, evaluation, closure. Design and execution together sit in Test Implementation and Execution phase (B).

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Test analysis and design". Analysis/design creates test conditions and cases but does not execute them.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Test implementation and execution". Implementation prepares environments and runs tests—matches 'designed and executed' together in practice.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Test planning and control". Planning sets scope and approach before detailed design.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Test closure". Closure archives results and metrics after execution completes.

37.studyTip: Tests designed and executed → Test Implementation and Execution (B).

38.overview: Queues are FIFO: enqueue at rear, dequeue from front—exactly the stem's description. Stacks are LIFO; deques allow both ends.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Deque". Deque allows both ends; not the narrow front-delete rear-insert definition.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Binary search tree". BST is ordered tree, not FIFO policy.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "Queue". Queue matches FIFO operations.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Stack". Stack deletes from same end it inserts (top).

39.overview: Quality attributes trade off: security vs performance, modifiability vs deployment complexity. Achieving one attribute can help or hurt others—both positive and negative effects (D).

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "The achievement of quality attribute will always have a negative effect". Attributes do not always harm the product—overstated.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "It is non deterministic". Outcomes are not purely non-deterministic lottery—engineering tradeoffs exist.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "The achievement of quality attribute will always have a positive effect". Not always positive—caching helps performance but may hurt consistency.
options.D: Option D (CORRECT): "The achievement of quality attribute will have a positive as well as negative effect". Captures tradeoff reality in architecture (ATAM sensitivities).

39.studyTip: Quality attributes can help and hurt → both effects (D).

40.overview: Worms are standalone self-propagating malware; viruses attach to host files. Trojans need user install; trap doors are hidden access.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Trap door". Trap door is a secret bypass, not standalone propagation.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Trojan horse". Trojan disguises as legitimate software, still needs host install.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Virus". Virus infects host programs—requires host file.
options.D: Option D (CORRECT): "Worm". Worm spreads independently across networks without attaching to a single host program.

40.studyTip: Independent malware without host program → worm (D).

41.overview: OSI Session layer manages dialog control (half-duplex/full-duplex) and synchronization checkpoints for long transfers.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Network layer". Network layer handles routing and logical addressing.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Session layer". Session layer provides dialog and synchronization services.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Data link layer". Data link handles hop-to-hop frames.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Transport layer". Transport handles end-to-end segments (TCP).

41.studyTip: Dialog control and synchronization → Session layer (B).

42.overview: Big data: volume, velocity, variety—datasets too large/complex for traditional tools. Definition matches big data (C).

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Wisdom". Wisdom is DIKW top level, not dataset definition.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Tiny data". Tiny data is opposite of the stem.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "Big data". Big data is the industry term for large complex datasets beyond legacy tools.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Information". Information is generic; big data is specific scale/complexity class.

42.studyTip: Large complex sets beyond traditional tools → big data (C).

62.overview: One-to-one cardinality: each entity on A maps to at most one on B and vice versa—option C definition.

options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "An entity in A maps to at most one in B; an entity in B may map to many in A". Describes one-to-many from A to B.

options.D: Option D (CORRECT): "Open design". Open design is explicit opposite of relying on secrecy of mechanism.

63.studyTip: Opposite of security through obscurity → open design (D).

97.overview: 3DES applies DES three times on 64-bit blocks with 56-bit keys (effective 168-bit key), strengthening legacy DES.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Using 144-bit blocks with a single DES pass". 144-bit block single pass is not 3DES.

options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Using only 128-bit blocks with two DES passes". 128-bit block description mismatches DES block size.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Replacing DES with AES in one round". AES replacement is different algorithm.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "IOException". IOException is checked—compiler enforces handling.

options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "NegativeArraySizeException". NegativeArraySizeException is unchecked runtime.

99.overview: Dijkstra critical-region conditions forbid assuming specific CPU speeds or processor count—algorithms must work generally. Assuming speeds/CPUs (B) is a false assumption.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "No process outside its critical region may block others indefinitely". Progress requirement is valid.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Assumptions may be made about CPU speeds and number of processors". Must not assume relative speeds or number of CPUs—violates fairness generality.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "No process waits forever to enter its critical region". Bounded waiting is desired, not false.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "No two processes are simultaneously inside their critical regions". Mutual exclusion on critical region is required.

99.studyTip: False critical-region assumption → about CPU speeds/count (B).

100.overview: A* with admissible heuristic is optimal; worst-case time can grow exponentially in search depth. Greedy best-first is not optimal; UCS lacks heuristic guidance but is optimal with nonnegative costs.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "A* Search". A* optimal with admissible heuristic, exponential worst case in many graphs—answer.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Uniform Cost Search". UCS optimal but lacks heuristic; exponential worst case also possible.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Iterative Deepening Search". IDS is complete/optimal in unweighted settings with repeated depth limits.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Greedy Best-First Search". Greedy best-first not optimal—fails optimality requirement in stem.

100.studyTip: Optimal informed search, exponential worst case → A* (A).
